title: Want People to Say Yes? Influence Starts with Empathy
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that influence at work begins with empathy: understanding the audience's language, priorities and doubts before presenting an idea. Using four personal stories, a failed jargon-heavy interview, a data proposal that got a neutral okay from her manager, an air-conditioning sales pitch that was all about the seller, and objections that should be handled in advance, she shows how pitches fail when they centre the speaker. Her fixes are mirroring the audience's vocabulary, asking what is in it for them, gathering qualitative input to build buy-in, and defusing objections early. The writing is anecdotal and aimed at tech professionals, with a subscriber upsell at the end.
points: Mirroring an audience's vocabulary and tempo signals alignment; mismatched jargon cost her a job advance.
Frame proposals around the decision-maker's priorities and KPIs, not the elegance of your data.
Casual conversations with the people affected can supply qualitative evidence and build buy-in before the formal ask.
A pitch centred on the seller fails; asking about the other person's priorities first is the corrective.
Consider your position relative to the person who may object and pre-empt objections about price, time and change.
quotes: I did not advance to the panel interview because I killed my pitch for the role. My background was a near-perfect match for the role, but it did not gel.
My empathy in communication was failing. I was not picking up on my audience or speaking his language.
Early in my career, I would go head-in with the data, assuming that was all that was needed. If the numbers were there, I figured that would be enough.

My failure here was that I was not framing it around his priorities or those of the department. What was getting better data of any interest to them if it did not result in better attainment towards one of the 7 (I know, too long a list) KPIs they had to hit, one of them being revenue goals? I needed to go in as an empathy catalyst. I needed to think about my audience.

So, I went outside the hard data. I started to ask reps about their process. During their downtime between calls with prospective customers calling in, I had casual conversations out in the cubicles, finding out how their days were. Inevitably, I got tidbits of qualitative data along the way.

Their pitch failed. It was about their company, its owner, and bright marketing materials, not about my goals (a package in my price range) and priorities (an air-conditioning system) with minimal disruption to my home.

Make the idea about them and solve their pain point. Avoid using jargon to sound smart. It might just confuse them or come off as arrogant. Frame the ideas around their priorities. Why sell an idea of a new product that is heavily discounted when the priority is functionality? And, of course, handle the objections before they happen.
